policy-short-run-s1.title: Sundra in a recession (invented country)
policy-short-run-s1.text: Sundra, an invented country, is in a recession. Real GDP is below full-employment output, and the unemployment rate is 8 percent while the natural rate is 5 percent. Sundra's central bank operates in an ample-reserves framework: it steers its policy rate with the interest rate it pays on reserve balances. Sundra's legislature can also change government spending or taxes.

policy-short-run-s2.title: Country Z after a fall in aggregate demand (invented)

policy-short-run-s3.title: Policy actions in four invented countries

table.caption: Fiscal and central bank actions in four invented countries
rows: Lowers the interest rate on reserve balances (ample)
Raises the interest rate on reserve balances (ample)

items.q: Which action by Sundra's central bank would move real GDP back toward full employment?
options: Sell government bonds to drain reserves
Lower the interest rate it pays on reserve balances
Raise the interest rate it pays on reserve balances
Raise the required reserve ratio for banks

why.correct: In the ample-reserves framework the central bank moves the policy rate with its administered rates. Lowering the interest rate on reserve balances lowers the policy rate, which starts the expansionary chain.
options: Selling bonds is a limited-reserves tool, and it is contractionary. With ample reserves, a change in the quantity of reserves in the flat part of reserve demand leaves the policy rate where it is.
Right: a lower administered rate pulls the policy rate down, loan rates fall, and investment and consumption rise, shifting AD right.
That raises the policy rate, which lowers investment and shifts AD left: the wrong direction in a recession.
A reserve requirement belongs to the limited-reserves framework, and raising it would be contractionary anyway.

items.q: Sundra's central bank lowers the interest rate it pays on reserve balances. Put the links of the chain in order, from the action to the result.
options: The interest rate on reserve balances falls
The policy rate falls
Loan rates and other interest rates fall
Investment and interest-sensitive consumption rise
Aggregate demand shifts right
Real GDP rises and unemployment falls

why.correct: Tool, policy rate, other interest rates, interest-sensitive spending, AD, then output and unemployment. Each link causes the next; a written answer that skips one loses the point.

items.q: Suppose Sundra's legislature cuts personal income taxes instead. What is the first link in the chain from the tax cut to AD?
options: Disposable income rises, so households spend more
The policy rate falls, so firms borrow more
Production costs fall for firms, so SRAS shifts right
Potential output rises, so LRAS shifts right

why.correct: The fiscal chain for taxes runs: taxes fall, disposable income rises, consumption rises (by the MPC times the tax cut), AD shifts right, then output rises and unemployment falls.
options: Right: a tax cut leaves households more after-tax income, and part of it is spent (the MPC), which raises consumption and AD.
A tax cut is fiscal policy; it does not work through the central bank's policy rate.
A cut in personal income taxes changes what households can spend. It is a demand-side change.
In the short-run model the tax cut works through spending. LRAS depends on resources and technology.

items.q: Sundra's central bank lowers its administered rates and, at the same time, the legislature raises government spending. Compared with either policy alone, what happens to AD and to the interest rate?
options: AD rises by more; the interest rate falls for sure
AD rises by more; the interest rate rises for sure
AD rises by more; the effect on the interest rate is indeterminate
The effect on AD is indeterminate, and the interest rate falls for sure

why.correct: When two policies push AD the same way, the AD effect is clear and the interest rate effect is the one that depends on sizes.
options: The monetary move lowers the rate, but the higher spending and income raise the demand for money and for borrowing, which push it up.
The fiscal move pushes the rate up, but the lower administered rate pulls it down. Without the sizes you cannot say which wins.
Right: both policies push AD right. The spending rise pushes interest rates up while the monetary move pushes them down, so the net change in the interest rate cannot be told without sizes.
Both policies are expansionary, so they push AD the same way. It is the interest rate whose change is unclear.

items.q: An economy has an inflationary gap, and its central bank operates with ample reserves. Build the chain for the right monetary policy.

why.correct: Raising the administered rate raises the policy rate; higher borrowing costs lower investment, so AD shifts left and the price level and real output fall.

specific.frame: The central bank ___ the interest rate on reserve balances, so the policy rate ___. Borrowing costs more, so ___ falls, AD shifts ___, and ___ fall.
specific.model: The central bank raises the interest rate on reserve balances, so the policy rate rises. Borrowing costs more, so investment falls, which shifts AD left, and as a result the price level and real output fall toward full employment.

policy.label: The action
options: raises
lowers

why.1: Lowering it is expansionary; an inflationary gap needs a contractionary move.

rate.label: The policy rate
options: rises
falls

why.1: The policy rate follows the administered rate up.

spending.label: The spending that falls
options: investment
government spending
potential output

why.1: Monetary policy works through interest-sensitive private spending, not the government budget.
why.2: Potential output is set by resources and technology, not by the policy rate.

direction.label: Which way AD shifts
options: left
right

why.1: Less spending at each price level is a shift left.

price.label: What falls
options: the price level and real output
full-employment output

why.1: Full-employment output (LRAS) does not move in the short run; the equilibrium moves along SRAS.

items.q: The graph shows Country Z after aggregate demand fell from AD1 to AD2. LRAS marks full-employment output. What does the new short-run equilibrium show?
options: An inflationary gap: output is above full employment
No gap: output is still at full employment
A recessionary gap with unemployment below the natural rate
A recessionary gap: output is below full employment

why.correct: Read the gap from where AD and SRAS cross relative to LRAS: to the left is a recessionary gap.
options: The new equilibrium is to the left of LRAS, not to the right.
Output moved away from LRAS when AD fell.
In a recessionary gap unemployment is above the natural rate, not below it.
Right: AD2 crosses SRAS to the left of LRAS, so real GDP is below full-employment output.

items.q: Which pair of policies would both push AD from AD2 back toward AD1?
options: A rise in taxes and a lower policy rate
A cut in taxes and a lower policy rate
A cut in government spending and a higher policy rate
A rise in government spending and a higher policy rate

why.correct: To close a recessionary gap both tools point the same way: more government spending or lower taxes, and a lower policy rate.
options: The tax rise lowers consumption and works against the lower policy rate.
Right: both are expansionary. The tax cut raises consumption; the lower policy rate raises investment.
Both are contractionary: they would push AD further left.
The higher policy rate lowers investment and works against the spending rise.

items.q: Suppose Country Z uses no policy at all. What happens to its economy in the long run?
options: Nominal wages rise, SRAS shifts left, and output returns to full employment
LRAS shifts left to meet the lower level of output
Nominal wages fall, SRAS shifts right, and output returns to full employment
AD shifts back right on its own as the price level falls

why.correct: Self-adjustment works through SRAS: in a recessionary gap, falling nominal wages and input prices shift SRAS right. Policy is used because that process can be slow.
options: Wages rise when unemployment is below the natural rate. Here it is above it, and a leftward SRAS shift would lower output further.
Full-employment output depends on resources and technology; a fall in spending does not move it.
Right: unemployment above the natural rate pushes nominal wages and other input prices down, so SRAS shifts right until output reaches full employment.
A fall in the price level is a movement along AD, not a shift of it. The long-run fix comes from SRAS.

items.q: Country Z's recessionary gap is 200 billion dollars and its MPC is 0.75. By how much would government spending have to rise to close the gap, in billions of dollars?

why.correct: The spending multiplier is $\frac{1}{1 - 0.75} = 4$. Divide the gap by it: $200 \div 4 = 50$ billion dollars of new government spending.

mistakes.why: You multiplied the gap by the multiplier. The multiplier makes each dollar of spending count several times, so divide the gap by it: 200 / 4 = 50.
You divided by the MPC. Divide by the spending multiplier, 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4.

items.q: In which countries do the fiscal and central bank actions push AD in opposite directions? Select all that apply.
options: Bela
Coro
Dren
Esk

why.correct: Dren and Esk mix an expansionary action with a contractionary one, so the net effect on AD depends on their sizes.
options: Both of Bela's actions are expansionary, so they push AD the same way.
Both of Coro's actions are contractionary, so they push AD the same way.
Right: the tax cut raises AD, but selling bonds shrinks the money supply, raises interest rates and lowers AD.
Right: the spending cut lowers AD, but buying bonds expands the money supply, lowers interest rates and raises AD.

items.q: In Coro, what happens to the policy rate, investment and the price level?
options: The policy rate rises, investment rises, the price level rises
The policy rate falls, investment rises, the price level falls
The policy rate is unchanged, investment falls, the price level falls
The policy rate rises, investment falls, the price level falls

why.correct: Contractionary monetary policy with ample reserves: higher administered rate, higher policy rate, less investment, AD left, lower price level and output.
options: A higher rate makes borrowing dearer, so investment falls, not rises.
Raising the interest rate on reserves raises the policy rate.
In the ample-reserves framework the policy rate follows the administered rates, so raising them raises the policy rate.
Right: a higher administered rate lifts the policy rate, borrowing costs rise, investment falls and AD shifts left, lowering the price level.

items.q: In Bela, which variable's change cannot be determined without knowing the sizes of the two policies?
options: Real output
The interest rate
The price level
The unemployment rate

why.correct: Two expansionary policies give a clear AD effect; their effects on the interest rate point opposite ways.
options: Both policies raise AD, so real output rises in the short run.
Right: higher spending pushes interest rates up while the lower administered rate pulls them down.
Both policies raise AD, so the price level rises.
Higher output means firms hire more, so unemployment falls.

items.q: Dren's central bank sells government bonds. On which graph is that action shown, and what does it show?
options: The money market: the money supply shifts left and the nominal interest rate rises
The reserve market: the administered rate rises and so does the policy rate
The loanable funds market: the supply of funds shifts right and the real interest rate falls
The money market: money demand shifts right and the nominal interest rate rises

why.correct: Match the tool to the framework: open market operations and the money market graph in limited reserves; administered rates and the reserve market graph in ample reserves.
options: Right: Dren uses the limited-reserves framework, so the bond sale shrinks the money supply on the money market graph.
That is the ample-reserves tool. Dren's table entry says it uses limited reserves and sells bonds.
The bond sale drains money from banks; it does not add to the supply of loanable funds.
A bond sale changes the quantity of money the central bank supplies, not how much money people want to hold.

items.q: Country Q has an inflationary gap: AD crosses SRAS to the right of LRAS. Its central bank, which operates with ample reserves, raises the interest rate on reserve balances. Shift the right curve and mark the new short-run equilibrium.

why.correct: The higher policy rate lowers investment, so AD shifts left; at the new equilibrium the price level and real output are lower.

key.because: a higher policy rate that lowers investment

slips.SRAS: A higher policy rate changes how much firms and households borrow and spend, so it shifts AD; it does not change production costs.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares fiscal and monetary policy in the short run?
options: Fiscal policy shifts AD; monetary policy shifts SRAS through interest costs
Monetary policy shifts AD in limited reserves but LRAS in ample reserves
Both shift AD; fiscal policy works through spending or taxes, monetary policy through interest rates
Both shift LRAS by changing how much the economy can produce

why.correct: Fiscal and monetary policy are both stabilization tools that shift AD; they differ in the first links of their chains.
options: Interest rates change borrowing and spending, so monetary policy shifts AD.
The framework changes the tool and the graph, not the curve the policy shifts.
Right: each is a demand-side tool, with a different first link in the chain.
Stabilization policy aims at spending in the short run; LRAS depends on resources and technology.

items.q: A rise in government spending raises real GDP and the price level. On the money market graph, what happens, and why?
options: Money supply rises because the government is spending more money, so the nominal interest rate falls
Money demand rises, as more output at higher prices takes more money, so the nominal rate rises
Money demand falls because higher prices make money worth less, so the nominal interest rate falls
Money supply falls because the government borrows from banks, so the nominal interest rate rises

why.correct: Expansionary fiscal policy raises money demand (more transactions at higher prices), which pushes the nominal interest rate up. That is why the interest rate effect of a policy mix can be unclear.
options: The central bank sets the money supply; government spending does not shift it.
Right: more nominal spending raises the transaction demand for money; with money supply fixed, the nominal interest rate rises.
Higher prices mean people need more money for the same purchases, not less.
Government borrowing shows up in the loanable funds market, not as a shift in the money supply.

items.q: An economy has an inflationary gap. Select every action that would shift AD to the left.
options: Raising income taxes
Raising the interest rate on reserve balances (ample reserves)
Buying government bonds on the open market (limited reserves)
Raising transfer payments to households

why.correct: Contractionary fiscal policy (higher taxes, lower spending or transfers) and contractionary monetary policy (a higher policy rate, or a bond sale with limited reserves) shift AD left.
options: Right: lower disposable income lowers consumption.
Right: a higher policy rate lowers investment and interest-sensitive consumption.
Buying bonds adds to the money supply and lowers interest rates: that is expansionary.
More transfers raise disposable income and consumption: that is expansionary.
